title: Reverb ↔ Space-Time — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of Reverb ↔ Space-Time's rich face, its first round at Sketch tier: four made pieces, each walking up to a test of a claim the page makes (an echo late by its path and Sabine's decay against a modelled room, a delay that becomes a place and then a colour, Lucier's loop against the box's computed modes, and the page's own where-are-you), with the fingerprint of the words each was laid against. I grow when the page is rewritten or a piece has something new to test; I never hold the entry's words.

offers.what: "A wall 10 meters away returns its reflection 29 milliseconds late" halves the path: the sound goes there and back, 20 m, so a wall 10 m away answers at 58.3 ms; 29 ms is a 10 m path, a wall 5 m away (the clap piece, step 1, and checks.mjs). The section's own bathroom (5–10 ms, walls 0.9–1.7 m) and cathedral (50–100 ms, walls 8.6–17 m) figures already use the round trip. Proposed: "A wall 5 meters away returns its reflection 29 milliseconds late", or "A reflection that travels 10 meters arrives 29 milliseconds late."

"a cathedral's first reflection at 50–100ms": in the model the floor answers first in every room, at about 9 ms for a clap at standing height, so the cue the sentence means is the first reflection off the walls. Proposed: "a cathedral's first wall reflection at 50–100ms" (and the same word for the bathroom).

Loudon's comment asks how room dimensions and room size work together and how well they represent real spaces. What the clap piece measured, in a 12 × 8 × 5 m box at α 0.2: size sets the decay, every side ×2 took Sabine from 0.99 to 1.97 s and the box's first 15 dB from 0.99 to 1.98 s, and the first wall echo from 19.6 to 39.2 ms. Shape sets the arrival pattern and Sabine barely sees it: at the same volume, low and wide (17.0 × 11.3 × 2.5 m) Sabine says 0.74 s, the box decays at 0.97 s over its first 15 dB and 1.56 s after. Surfaces set the decay and leave the arrivals alone (tile: Sabine 6.57 s, first wall echo still 19.6 ms). Sabine matched the box's first 15 dB within about 5% for the near-cubic room at every α tried, and ran short of its later decay, more so when the room is flat. Proposed, after the Sabine sentence: "Size and surfaces set how long the room rings; its dimensions set when the first walls answer. Sabine sees shape only as surface area, so it fits a room near a cube with absorption spread evenly, and misses a long or low one."

The Haas sentence is right on headphones and leaves out what the delay costs in mono, which the haas piece makes audible: summed to one channel, a 10–30 ms delay becomes a comb filter, silent at 1⁄(2Δt) and every 1⁄Δt after (at 25 ms: 20, 60, 100 Hz…, 500 notches below 20 kHz). The same time difference becomes place in two ears and timbre in one, the page's own space–time–frequency triangle and its mirror link to Frequency-Time Duality. Proposed, after the Haas sentence: "Sum the two speakers to mono and the same delay becomes a comb filter: time difference becomes timbre." Also unverified by the piece and left to Loudon: where one sound splits into two depends on the sound, under 10 ms for clicks, nearer 50 for speech (Litovsky et al., 1999, from memory, not re-read this round).

"Each iteration emphasizes room's natural frequencies" holds, with a condition the sitting-in-a-box piece measured in a 6 × 4.5 × 2.6 m box (Sabine 1.04 s, Schroeder frequency 244 Hz): below the Schroeder frequency each surviving peak is one computed mode (the 8 strongest sit 0.21 Hz from one, random frequencies 1.06 Hz) and holds when the microphone moves (+15.1 dB above the band median here, +7.5 dB moved). Above it about 46 modes overlap inside each peak at 1 kHz, so what survives is set by where the loudspeaker and microphone stand: the same frequencies fall from +10.3 to +3.3 dB when the microphone moves, and the tone that wins after 32 passes moves from 1885.8 to 1228.1 Hz. Without a loudspeaker band in the loop the room alone ends on its lowest mode, 28.6 Hz (1, 0, 0), with the microphone in the first place. Proposed for "What's happening": "Each iteration emphasizes the room's natural frequencies as heard from where the loudspeaker and microphone stand; the loudspeaker is part of the loop, so part of the room."

verdicts.file: Reverb ↔ Space-Time — rich — one clap, one room.html
verdicts.why: A real test that caught the 29 ms slip; numbers reproduce independently. But 'Sabine barely sees it' misreads its own figures (Sabine moves 0.99→0.74 s; the box's first 15 dB barely moves, its late decay lengthens), the two-slope decay is the bare specular box's and only the fine print says so, and the floor is 7.3 ms in the low room, not 9: fix the heading, add a 'how far a box stands for a real room' paragraph (the second half of Loudon's comment), say 7–9 ms.

pieces.file: Reverb ↔ Space-Time — rich — one clap, one room.html
pieces.title: one clap, one room · four steps
pieces.caption: **Loudon's question, played: how do a room's dimensions and its size work together?** The page's clap experiment built up from one wall: an echo late by its path (drag the wall), six walls writing the room's dimensions in time, every echo of a shoebox room with Sabine's RT60 beside the box's own decay, and last the test. Size sets how long the room rings, shape sets when the walls answer, and surfaces set the decay without moving the arrivals. It also checks the section's numbers: a wall 10 m away answers at 58 ms, not 29.

verdicts.file: Reverb ↔ Space-Time — rich — a delay becomes a place.html
verdicts.why: Walks up from ITD to Haas to a split the reader finds, which can fall outside the page's 10–30 ms; comb numbers right (25 ms: 20, 60, 100 Hz…, 500 notches). Note: the page's sentence is about loudspeakers and the piece is on headphones, disclosed; cite the thresholds to Wallach 1949 and Blauert, not Litovsky 1999 unread.

pieces.by: Web Audio · two ears, one delay
pieces.near: The Haas Effect makes this visceral
pieces.title: a delay becomes a place · four steps · headphones
pieces.caption: **The Haas sentence on headphones.** The same click in both ears, then the right ear late by under a millisecond (the sound walks across your head), then 1 to 40 ms (it stays put and widens), and last the test: push on until you hear two, then sum the ears to one and hear the same delay turn into a comb filter. Time becomes place in two ears and colour in one.

verdicts.file: Reverb ↔ Space-Time — rich — sitting in a box.html
verdicts.why: A real test the page passes; 0.21 Hz reproduces. Words overstate it: overlap is 0.9 at 141 Hz and 2.75 at 244, so 'one each' holds only below ~140 Hz; a local random baseline gives 0.71 Hz, not 1.06; both peak sets drop ~7 dB when the mic moves (6 dB over chance below, 2 above), so 'hold' against 'sink' overstates; 28.6 Hz is mic-here only and under the 30 Hz high-pass. Reword caption and verdict; engine stays.

pieces.file: Reverb ↔ Space-Time — rich — sitting in a box.html
pieces.title: sitting in a box · after Lucier · four steps
pieces.caption: **Lucier's loop as arithmetic.** A voice once through a modelled room, the room's own peaks against the modes its dimensions predict, the voice through the loop up to forty times, and last the test of the page's claim that the room's natural frequencies emerge. They do. Below about 244 Hz each survivor is one mode; above it, which tones survive depends on where the loudspeaker and microphone stand.

verdicts.file: Reverb ↔ Space-Time — rich — where are you.html
verdicts.why: The blind round offers only the page's own place-names, then tells the reader 'notice what you named: a place, not an amount of reverb', which it couldn't fail. Add a free-words box (or non-place choices) and let the verdict read what was written; fix '3 m in every room' (2.48 m in the small room).

pieces.file: Reverb ↔ Space-Time — rich — where are you.html
pieces.title: where are you · four steps
pieces.caption: **The demonstration, with you as the student.** One voice dry, then in a small room, a hall and a cathedral, each drawn to one scale, the voice 3 m from you in every room. Then the four again in a shuffled order, and the page's question: where are you? Answer each, then see where you were.
